sections.title: Decode it live
sections.intro: The interviewer leans in: "Tell me about a time you had to make a call without all the information you wanted." Before you say a word, decode it.

questions.prompt: What shape of question is this?
options: A values question — they want your philosophy
A past-behavior question — they want one real story
A hypothetical — they want your general approach
A technical question — they want the decision itself
questions.explanation: "Tell me about a time…" asks for a specific past event, because past behavior is the best predictor they have. Answering with "generally, I'd…" dodges what they asked for.

questions.prompt: Which signal area is this primarily testing?
options: Ambiguity — moving forward with incomplete information
Ownership — driving the problem end-to-end
Perseverance — pushing through a hard obstacle
Scope — the size of the problem you handled
questions.explanation: "Without all the information" is the tell. A good story will touch others too, but if the ambiguity isn't center stage, you've answered a different question.

questions.prompt: What do candidates most often *under-tell* in an Ambiguity story?
options: How they created clarity, and how they checked it after
How quickly they made the final decision
How uncertain and stressful the situation felt
Who on the team was responsible for the gap
questions.explanation: Saying "it was ambiguous" isn't the signal. Showing *how* you reduced the uncertainty (data, conversations, a quick prototype) and then validated your assumptions is.

questions.prompt: The company publishes values like "Bias for Action." How should that change your answer?
options: Ignore it — values never affect the scoring
Mention as many of their values as you can
Let it shape word choice where it fits naturally
Name the value explicitly in your opening line
questions.explanation: Values are mostly the same signal areas in company vocabulary. Forcing them in ("value-dropping") is obvious to trained interviewers. At a company that genuinely runs on its values, like Amazon, the exact language matters more.

questions.prompt: You're interviewing for a senior role. Your best ambiguity story is from your first year, a small ticket. What's the risk?
options: None — any honest example scores the same
Scope — a junior-sized story can get you downleveled
Recency — interviewers dislike older stories
Relevance — the story isn't really about ambiguity
questions.explanation: Story choice is itself a Scope signal. A small-box story tells them you operate in a small box, even if you tell it perfectly.

questions.prompt: Mid-story, you realize it also shows you persuading a skeptical manager. What do you do with that?
options: Make it the main thread of the story instead
Cut it — stick strictly to the asked signal
Save it and tell it as a separate story later
Mention it briefly — it's real Leadership signal
questions.explanation: One strong story usually hits several signal areas. Keep the requested one at the center, and surface the others briefly as threads they can follow up on.

sections.title: Spot the problem
sections.intro: Each one stands alone. What's the candidate getting wrong, or what's being tested?

questions.prompt: Opening line of a conflict answer:
questions.snippet: "Honestly, I'm not really one to create conflict — I get along with pretty much everyone."
options: It's too short — they should add more context
It signals avoidance — tech values healthy conflict
It's too modest — they should sound more confident
It's fine — it shows they're easy to work with
questions.explanation: It reads as junior, or as someone who avoids hard conversations. Interviewers want to see you initiate disagreement constructively, not stay out of it.

questions.prompt: "What would you do if your manager asked you to cut a feature to hit a deadline?" What shape is this, and what does it test?
options: Values — your philosophy on deadlines in general
Technical — how you'd re-scope the feature
Past-behavior — they want a real story about it
Hypothetical — your judgment where experience is thin
questions.explanation: Hypotheticals test reasoning. Grounding your answer in a real similar experience still helps, because it shows the judgment isn't theoretical.

questions.snippet: "I basically lived at the office for three weeks — nights, weekends, whatever it took — and we hit the date."
options: Strong — it proves real commitment to the team
Off-topic — this is actually an Ownership story
Too short — needs more detail on the hours
A martyr story — reads as poor planning, not grit
questions.explanation: Raw hours aren't the signal. Creative problem-solving under pressure is. Knowing when to change the plan, or even quit, is strong Perseverance signal too.

questions.snippet: "I'd say I care too much about getting things perfect."
options: Too negative — they should pick something smaller
Fine, as long as they deliver it confidently
A humble-brag — no real downside, no real Growth signal
Ideal — it's honest without hurting their chances
questions.explanation: Growth signal comes from a real mistake, a specific lesson, and changed behavior afterward. Avoid the other extreme too: a mistake so basic for your level that it raises maturity doubts.

questions.prompt: Two candidates describe the same project:
questions.snippet:
A: "We aligned on the proposal."
B: "I messaged the tech lead directly given how sensitive it was, then presented to the whole team once we were aligned."
options: A — B over-explains a minor detail
B — it shows how and when they communicated
Equal — both describe the same outcome
A — it's more concise and team-focused
questions.explanation: Communication is scored on the *how* and *when*: channel choice, audience, sequencing. "We aligned" hides all of it, and the "we" hides who did the work.

questions.prompt: A candidate moves from a traditional enterprise to a fast-moving tech company, gives solid answers, and gets an offer one level below what they expected. Which lens most likely caused it?
options: Question types — they misread the questions
Company values — they forgot to name them
Cultural assessment — behaviors didn't read right there
Signal areas — the answers lacked real signal
questions.explanation: Interviewers unconsciously compare you to the successful people they already know. The same skill can read differently depending on how you talk about hierarchy, results, and speed vs. quality.
